page.title: NIS2 Risk Assessment
page.subtitle: Seven questions per system. Risk level and audit-defensible justification per BSI Grundschutz 200-2.
page.metaTitle: NIS2 Risk Assessment - free, no signup
page.metaDescription: Score your IT systems per BSI Grundschutz 200-2 in under 5 minutes. Three domains (Security, Operational, Compliance) with the maximum principle. Audit-defensible justification per axis.

hero.headline: NIS2 Risk Assessment
hero.subhead: Seven questions per system. Risk level and audit-defensible justification per BSI Grundschutz 200-2.

intro.trustLine: BSI-200-2 maximum principle. NIS2 Art 21(1) + Art 21(2)(a), BSIG §30. No signup, the result stays with you.
intro.inventoryHint: Once you have your inventory from Lesson 2.2 of our CEO course, every asset takes under a minute.

example.label: Example result
example.tierExplanation: Standard, driven by internet exposure and customer data. The platform writes the per-axis justification ready for management sign-off.

security.label: Cyber attack surface
security.description: How exposed is the system to attack?

operational.label: Operational dependency
operational.description: How critical is the system to ongoing operations?

basis.label: Basic
basis.description: Risk acceptance with management sign-off allowed. Basic measures sufficient.

standard.label: Standard
standard.description: Standard Grundschutz Bausteine apply. Full implementation required.

kern.label: Core
kern.description: Elevated risk level. BSI-200-3 risk analysis required, external support recommended.

internetExposure.question: How is the system reachable from the internet?

offline.label: Fully offline, no network connection
offline.why: The system has no network connection. External attack vectors are eliminated. Internal and physical threats remain relevant.

internalOnly.label: Internal network only, no internet access
internalOnly.why: The system is reachable only on the internal network. External attack surface minimal, internal threats (compromised endpoints, insiders) remain relevant. Grundschutz NET.1.1 applies.

vpn.label: Reachable only via VPN
vpn.why: The system is reachable only via VPN. Authentication security of remote access is critical. Grundschutz NET.3.3 (VPN) and ORP.4 (identity management) apply. NIS2 Art 21(2)(j) (multi-factor authentication) proportionate.

internetExposed.label: Directly reachable from the internet
internetExposed.why: The system is directly reachable from the internet. High attack surface from mass and targeted attacks. Grundschutz NET.1.1, NET.3.2 (firewall) and OPS.1.1.5 (logging) apply. NIS2 Art 21(2)(e) (vulnerability handling) and Art 21(2)(h) (cryptography) proportionate.

userCount.question: Who has access to this system?

tiny.label: A few standard users (small team, no special privileges)
tiny.why: Small set of standard users without special privileges. Access controls operationally manageable. Grundschutz ORP.4 applies.

small.label: Many standard users (whole departments, all without special privileges)
small.why: Many users with standard permissions. Structured role management and regular access reviews required. Grundschutz ORP.4 applies. NIS2 Art 21(2)(i) (access control policies) proportionate.

large.label: Includes privileged users (admins, finance, executives)
large.why: Privileged users have access. Attack value concentrates on few accounts. Strict role separation, multi-factor authentication on privileged accounts and regular access reviews required. Grundschutz ORP.4 and NIS2 Art 21(2)(j) (multi-factor authentication) proportionate.

externalToo.label: Includes external people (customers, suppliers, partners)
externalToo.why: External people have access. Identity verification and separation of internal/external permissions critical. NIS2 Art 21(2)(d) (supply chain security) and Art 21(2)(j) (multi-factor authentication) proportionate.

vendorSupport.question: Will security updates keep coming for this system?

active.label: Yes, the vendor actively maintains it and ships patches
active.why: Vendor active in the market, patches released promptly. Standard patch management sufficient. Grundschutz OPS.1.1.3 applies.

mature.label: Yes, but patches arrive only occasionally
mature.why: Vendor established, patches less frequent. Higher self-responsibility for monitoring. Grundschutz OPS.1.1.3 applies.

eolAnnounced.label: No, end of support has been announced
eolAnnounced.why: Vendor has announced end of support. Migration or compensating controls required. NIS2 Art 21(2)(e) (vulnerability handling) proportionate.

abandoned.label: No, vendor is gone or in-house build with no maintenance
abandoned.why: System without active support. High residual risks from unpatched vulnerabilities. Migration or replacement controls urgent.

incidentHistory.question: Any security incidents with this system in the last 3 years?

none.label: No incidents, and we have logging or monitoring that would catch them
none.why: No incidents documented and monitoring in place. Strongest position: the absence of incidents is substantiated by logs. NIS2 Art 21(2)(f) (effectiveness assessment) applied periodically.

minor.label: No known incidents, but we don't actively monitor the system
minor.why: No known incidents but no monitoring in place. The absence cannot be substantiated. Setting up basic logging is the first step. NIS2 Art 21(2)(f) (effectiveness assessment) recommended.

major.label: One past incident (minor or major)
major.why: One incident in the last 3 years. Lessons learned should be documented in writing. NIS2 Art 21(2)(b) (incident handling) applies. Grundschutz DER.2.1.

repeated.label: Multiple or recurring incidents
repeated.why: Multiple or recurring incidents. Structural weaknesses likely. Full risk reassessment and compensating controls required.

downtimeTolerance.question: How long until customers or operations notice this system is down?

weeks.label: Weeks. Nobody would really notice.
weeks.why: Operations can run for weeks without the system before customers or workflows notice. Low availability need. Standard backups sufficient.

days.label: Days. We'd manage with workarounds.
days.why: Operations tolerate days of outage with workarounds. Medium availability need. Grundschutz CON.3 (data backup) applies.

hours.label: Hours. Customers or operations would notice.
hours.why: Hours of outage cause noticeable restrictions for customers or operations. Higher availability need. Grundschutz CON.3, OPS.1.2.5 (remote maintenance) and emergency planning apply.

minutes.label: Minutes. Operations stop immediately.
minutes.why: Minutes of outage halt operations. Very high availability need. Redundancy, automatic failover and tested emergency plans required. NIS2 Art 21(2)(c) (business continuity) is load-bearing.

replaceability.question: If this system disappeared tonight, when would you be running with an equivalent? (Buying, restoring from backup, or rebuilding all count.)

oneDay.label: Within a day
oneDay.why: System quickly replaceable. Low residual risk on failure.

oneWeek.label: Within a week
oneWeek.why: Replacement possible within a week. Have workarounds ready for the transition.

oneMonth.label: Within a month
oneMonth.why: Replacement takes up to a month. Emergency planning for the transition period required. Grundschutz DER.4 (emergency management) applies.

irreplaceable.label: Not at all, or only as a long custom build
irreplaceable.why: System not or only custom-replaceable. Load-bearing operational risk. Emergency planning and protective measures central. NIS2 Art 21(2)(c) (business continuity) is load-bearing.

personalData.question: What kind of sensitive data does this system process?

none.label: No sensitive data (public or general business information only)
none.why: No personal or specially regulated data. GDPR and sector-specific rules don't apply heavily.

employeeOnly.label: Employee data (HR files, contracts, salaries)
employeeOnly.why: Employee data. GDPR applies. Standard TOMs per Art 32 GDPR applicable.

customer.label: Customer data or operational business data
customer.why: Customer or business data. GDPR applies plus commercial confidentiality. Standard TOMs and data processing agreements with external processors required.

sensitivePii.label: Sensitive data: Art 9 GDPR (health, religion) or regulated operational data (OT, KRITIS)
sensitivePii.why: Special personal data per Art 9 GDPR or regulated operational data (e.g. OT systems, KRITIS-related data). Elevated protection duty. Data protection impact assessment mandatory for Art 9 GDPR data. Extended technical and organisational measures required.

hardStops.heading: Hard-stops triggered
hardStops.intro: Some answers are so impactful that one alone elevates your risk level, regardless of the other six. This protects against under-classification under BSI's Maximum-Prinzip. Click each one for legal basis and what to do.

internetExposed.note: Internet exposure forces a minimum risk level of Standard in the Security domain.
internetExposed.what: An internet-reachable system cannot be classified as Basic. The threat model is automated scanning, mass exploitation campaigns, and targeted attacks against the public attack surface — even small assets get probed thousands of times per day.
internetExposed.legal: NIS2 Art 21(2)(e) (vulnerability handling) and Art 21(2)(h) (cryptography) make patching and TLS non-negotiable. BSIG §30(2) Nr. 5 and Nr. 8 transpose this. BSI Grundschutz NET.1.1 (network architecture), NET.3.2 (firewall), and OPS.1.1.5 (logging) are foundational for any internet-reachable asset and apply at Standard depth.
internetExposed.todo: Implement Standard-tier Security: hardware or cloud firewall, network segmentation, centralised logging, monthly patch cycle, TLS 1.2+ for external traffic. Document the firewall ruleset, the patch SLA, and the monitoring approach. The management body must sign off; §38 BSIG makes them accountable.

downtimeMinutes.note: Minutes-downtime threshold forces a minimum risk level of Standard in the Operational domain.
downtimeMinutes.what: A system whose loss halts operations within minutes cannot be classified as Basic. The threat model is operational disruption — ransomware, power outage, network failure — that breaches the continuity duties under Art 21(2)(c).
downtimeMinutes.legal: NIS2 Art 21(2)(c) explicitly names 'business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management' — backup and DR are named duties, not optional. BSIG §30(2) Nr. 3 transposes. BSI Grundschutz CON.3 (data backup) and DER.4 (emergency management) apply at Standard depth. Untested failover is the most common audit finding here.
downtimeMinutes.todo: Implement redundancy or automatic failover. Define RTO (recovery time objective) and RPO (recovery point objective), test them at least annually, and document the results. The BCP and the test report belong in the management body sign-off binder.

sensitivePii.note: Sensitive data (Art 9 GDPR or regulated operational data) forces risk level Core in the Compliance domain.
sensitivePii.what: Special-category personal data (Art 9 GDPR) or regulated operational data (OT, KRITIS) forces the Core tier. The data class itself drives the elevated protection duty, independent of the other six axes.
sensitivePii.legal: GDPR Art 9 sets the elevated protection duty for health, religion, biometric, and similar data. GDPR Art 35 makes a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) mandatory for high-risk processing — Art 9 data triggers this almost always. NIS2 Art 21(2)(h) (cryptography) becomes load-bearing. BSIG §30(2) Nr. 8 transposes. Critically, Core tier under BSI-200-2 §8.2 requires BSI-200-3 Risikoanalyse: a separate, scenario-based risk analysis on top of this assessment.
sensitivePii.todo: Run a BSI-200-3 Risikoanalyse for this asset. Run a GDPR Art 35 DPIA if Art 9 data is involved. Implement encryption at rest and in transit. Document extended TOMs (Art 32 GDPR). Involve your Data Protection Officer (DPO/DSB) and have the management body sign off.

result.heading: Risk assessment result
result.drivingDomainBody: The risk level is determined by the {domain} domain. Maximum principle per BSI-200-2 §8.2.
result.whySubtitle: These sentences are the basis of the risk-level justification. Use them unchanged or adapt them with the management body.
result.bausteineSubtitle: Indicative list of fitting Bausteine from the IT-Grundschutz catalogue. Final selection happens during modelling per BSI-200-2 §8.3.
result.measuresSubtitle: Art 21(2) NIS2 lists ten measures every entity in scope must implement ('shall include at least the following'). Implementation depth follows your risk level: Basic requires minimal evidence, Standard the full Grundschutz depth, Core an additional risk-specific deepening per BSI-200-3.
result.cirNote: For the 11 entity types in scope of CIR 2024/2690 (cloud computing services, data centres, MSPs and MSSPs, DNS providers, TLD registries, content delivery networks, online marketplaces, search engines, social networks, trust service providers), the Annex sets out detailed implementing rules. Other entities apply BSI Grundschutz as the recognised methodology.
result.signoffBody: This risk assessment is binding only with management body sign-off (§38 BSIG, Art 20 NIS2). Enter name, date and signature on the printed document.

chart.title: Risk assessment as a radar chart, grouped by domain

disclaimer.heading: Legal note
disclaimer.body: This risk assessment is an informational classification based on your inputs. It is not legal advice under the German RDG. The assessment becomes binding only with management body sign-off per §38 BSIG and Art 20 NIS2. The methodology follows BSI Grundschutz 200-2 §8.2 (Schutzbedarfsfeststellung) and the maximum principle; the provider does not warrant regulatory acceptance in any specific case.

a.label: Risk analysis and information system security policies

c.label: Business continuity (backup, disaster recovery) and crisis management

d.label: Supply chain security (supplier and service-provider relationships)

e.label: Security in acquisition, development and maintenance including vulnerability handling and disclosure

f.label: Policies and procedures to assess the effectiveness of risk-management measures

g.label: Basic cyber hygiene practices and cybersecurity training

h.label: Policies and procedures on the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption

i.label: Human resources security, access control policies and asset management

j.label: Multi-factor or continuous authentication, secured voice/video/text and secured emergency communications
